Follow the degree with a law degree. Then work for big oil or coal against the EPA.
This is a legitimate route. Pretty much any EPA regulation of consequence will end up in courts, often times facing competing lawsuits from both industry groups and environmental advocacy groups.

You can do a certain number of things with a BA in Environmental Science (wetlands delineations, Phase I Environmental Site Assessments that are required for commercial and industrial property transactions, collecting air or water samples, responding to spills). Unless you like working outside a lot, if you go the Environmental Science route, you would probably want an MA. If you go the Environmental Engineering route, you could get by with just a bachelor's degree.

"Environmental" is kind of a broad term which is good and bad (so is "business" for that matter). You don't have to be pigeonholed if you don't want to be. But if you find something you like doing (being out in the field, working in a lab, doing desktop research, designing contaminant treatment systems, responding to spill clean-ups) you can make a career of it.

The other good thing about the environmental field is that it requires a certain amount of boots on the ground, so it is relatively immune to outsourcing. Also, people will always need clean water and there are still a lot of contaminated sites out there, so I see I don't see a future where this industry disappears.

I don't know how well business and environment would go together as a degree. If you want to work in business as a career, you might want to major in business and just take a few environmental classes. The route I think you would be looking at there would be managing sustainability initiatives for corporations. I see that as being a point of emphasis over the next 10-20 years. There would continue to be a need for managing compliance, property acquisitions, and legacy contamination at these same companies. However, if you want to work in the environmental field with just a business background, I think you would be looking at being a project manager for large environmental projects (long-term clean ups, multi-national and/or multi-site audits). There is always the need for people to manage projects and clients in the environmental field.

I know you mentioned the EPA specifically. Working for government is another option. Keep in mind there are also state-level government agencies. I wouldn't necessarily recommend this route. If you do try and get hired by the EPA, they tend to want more than a bachelor's degree and they like lots of initials at the end of your name.

One other bit of advice is that in the environmental field, air is a much bigger segment than most people realize. By that I mean that most people think of water, waste, sludge, soil, toxic spills, etc when they think of environmental jobs. In reality, air regulations and requirements seem to take up about half of the overall effort in environmental compliance. Some 3rd-party organizations are split into two groups, one for just air and one for everything else. Lesson learned here is that if you concentrate somewhat on air in your studies, you might be in a better position to find a job when you graduate.

In any event, here are possible routes and example companies to work for if you got an environmental degree:

  • Consulting/engineering firms (e.g. ERM)

  • Spill response companies (e.g. Clean Harbors)

  • Industry (e.g. General Motors)

  • Government (e.g. EPA)

  • Advocacy (e.g. Greenpeace)
